A high resolution view of the whole cell

In 2020 a new, state-of-the-art super-resolution microscope will arrive at EMBL Heidelberg. This new addition to an already extensive range of microscopes will enable EMBL researchers to push the boundaries of what can be imaged. For example, by showing things in 3D at much higher resolution. Conventional light microscopy can resolve down to about 200 nanometres. This is more than enough to see a whole cell, but it’s not enough to distinguish individual proteins. New types of super-resolution microscopy allow researchers to see things down to a resolution of about 20 nanometres. However, even these methods have limitations. Commonly used super-resolution methods focus on a thin layer close to the cover glass on which a sample is placed. But, biological processes take place throughout the whole cell. “What researchers are really looking for is a high resolution across the whole cell, which can be around 10 micrometres thick,” says Jonas Ries, a group leader at EMBL Heidelberg. The new microscope being built will allow just that. It uses a super-resolution technology called Single-Molecule Localization Microscopy (SMLM). SMLM locates individual molecules with an extremely high precision of just a few nanometres. By taking thousands of images and adding them all together, a final super-resolution image is created. Crucial to the microscope’s ability to take these images deep inside a cell – up to around 100 micrometres – is its two objectives. While one objective is common in microscopy, using two allows more light to be captured and increases the resolution in 3D. A high-resolution 3D view of the whole cell will allow Ries and his group to answer fundamental biological questions about how things work. “Our main project is studying the processes that rearrange whole cells during endocytosis,” Ries explains. Endocytosis is the process cells take up fluids, molecules, and other substances. “This process is quite complicated, and involves many proteins moving and coming together. With this new microscope, we can image this in 3D at high resolution.” Building the microscope is a collaborative effort between the Ries group, EMBL’s mechanical and electronics workshops, the Advanced Light Microscopy Facility (ALMF), and Abbelight, a French start-up that specialises in super-resolution microscopy. EMBL researchers will soon be able to use the new microscope and benefit from its ultra-high resolution. “We are setting up the microscope as a service at the ALMF. The system is designed to be accessible to everyone,” says Ries. The build is funded as part of the European Research Council (ERC) grant that Ries received in 2017. As EMBL welcomes the building of the new world-class imaging centre (the EMBL Imaging Centre), this new microscope will ensure that EMBL remains at the forefront of imaging technology.
